title: Portuguese Oak: Ancient Portuguese Oaks You Can Visit
meta_description: The Iberian oak that holds its dead leaves all winter. Ours in the Sierra de Aracena is 27.5 metres tall on a trunk 3.10 metres round.
intro: The quejigo, as Spain calls the Portuguese oak, holds on to its dead leaves through winter and drops them only when the new ones push, so in February it is a brown tree in a bare landscape. The tallest one we know of stands below the Pena de Arias Montano, above the village of Alajar in the Sierra de Aracena. It is 27.5 metres high, which is what the Junta de Andalucia's register listed it for, and its two main limbs rise almost straight up from a trunk 3.10 metres round. South of Pamplona, Navarra declared a quejigo in the hill district of the Valdorba a Natural Monument in 2009 and published no measurements at all. In Lisbon, another fills an arcaded courtyard of the agronomy school in the Tapada da Ajuda, and a reader's photograph and their estimate of 96 years are all we have on it. Nobody else has put an age on any of the three.
